The clerk set her pen down in the ledger's groove and looked at him properly—the red eyes got half a second, no more, and the staff the rest. "Registering." She reached under the counter and brought up a slate, a stub of charcoal, and a sheet of paper that had faint lines of enchantment stitched through it, like threads of frost. "Right then. It's two silver, once, and it buys you this: a contract slip that's keyed to you, the right to take work off that board, and the Guild's certification when your Level rises. We don't set your Rank—that's your Power, we just read it. Guild Rank's separate. You'd start at Novice, same as everyone." She turned the slate toward him. He pulled the long sheet off its hook and took it to the counter. The clerk read the wardens' seal upside down before he'd fully laid it out, and her pen paused over the ledger. "The catacombs." She said it the way she might say a weather report. "Solo, is it?" She didn't wait for an answer; she was already writing. "Your funeral's free, we don't charge for those." She inked a line, blotted it, then took the slip from him, stamped it with the Guild's crossed swords, and slid it back across the counter. "There. Logged as active. Slip stays with you—when Level 1's cleared, the seal goes READY on its own, you bring it back here, and we settle sixty copper for the level." She looked up at last, and there was something almost like interest in it. "It's restless dead down there, upper galleries. Wardens seal the stair when they're done with a floor, so you'll know what's cleared and what isn't. Ruined chapel marks the entrance, hour west along the road." She nodded toward the side door. "West gate's that way. Ask the gate wardens for the Old Crown road and they'll point you." The pen went back to the ledger. "And Novice—if the slip comes back with your name on it but you don't, we'd like to know that too. Saves paperwork." The dice players had started a new round. Somewhere behind the hall, a kettle whistled.

The side door let him into a lane that ran down toward the west gate, and the gate wardens pointed him with a jerk of a chin once the Guild slip showed: the Old Crown road, past the sheep pens, keep to the left where it forked. The road was packed earth, wheel-rutted, running between hedgerows that smelled of crushed green growth and warmed dust. The morning had burnt off its damp by the time Alderwatch's walls fell behind him, and traffic thinned with them—a carter, then nothing but birdsong and the tick of his own boots. The ruined chapel showed itself after a while as a broken tooth against the trees: a roof half gone, walls of mossy stone, a doorless archway that stood open like a mouth. He was still a quarter mile off when he heard the swearing. A man sat on the roadside bank ahead, one leg stuck out in front of him at an angle that was trying very hard to look casual and not quite managing it. Forties, mud to the knee, a handcart loaded with bundled firewood tipped over beside him and its wheel still turning slowly. A dog—curly, wiry, unbothered—stood over him panting. "Oi." The man waved. "You there. You a walking sort, or just dressed like one?" He tried to push himself up, hissed, and sat back down on the bank. "Cart went over on the rut there and my ankle went with it. Wood's not heavy, it's the getting up that's the problem." He squinted at the staff, then at the road behind Alaric, empty both ways. "Quarter mile to the chapel, that's where you're headed, isn't it—everyone your sort is. Well. I'm not asking you to carry me to town, that's mad. But if you'd help me up and get the cart righted, I can hobble. Maybe lean. My girl's at the chapel cottage—her mother keeps it, they sell candles to the visitors, such as there are." He paused, and added, less easily: "Name's Bren. And I'd owe you one, which I know is worth what it's worth, from a man sat in a ditch."

"You do that," Bren said, and meant it, which was as far as the ditch-man's dignity would carry him. The girl—Nella, her mother called her through the doorway—was already coming down the path, wiping her hands on her apron, whether to help her father or to play guide it wasn't clear until she did both. "This way, then. It's just the arch, you'd find it yourself, but Mam says I'm to show you the stair." The chapel's interior was cooler than the road by several degrees, and darker; the candles in the cottage window suddenly made sense. Pigeons clattered out through the broken roof as they crossed the nave, and their droppings had streaked the old floorstones white. Behind the shattered altar, stone steps went down into the earth, wide enough for two, worn in the middle like a riverbed. An iron brazier stood at the head of them, cold. "Wardens light it when they work the top floor," Nella said, following his look. "It's been out a while. Past the stair it's the upper galleries—long rooms with the burial niches in the walls, and side doors off them. The wardens' seal is a painted line across the arch, red and white. Where you see the line, that floor's done and you don't need to go past it." She looked at him sidelong. "Da said you're clearing it. The whole level. Alone?" She didn't wait for an answer; she pointed at the dark. "There's a second stair partway along, goes down to Level 2. Don't take that one by mistake." Then she turned back toward the cottage, because there was a cart to unload and a father to bully, and the dog followed her, and Alaric stood at the head of the steps with cold air breathing up past his ankles, carrying the smell of wet stone and old dust. The first steps went down out of the daylight. Below, the stair turned once and ended at a landing where a corridor ran left and right into the dark, the beginnings of two galleries, both silent.

The second wave tore out of him and the half-ring broke apart. The blade-bearer on his left simply ceased—bones bursting apart mid-swing, the rusted sword ringing off the flags and spinning away. The second came apart a heartbeat later, ribs and skull scattering, its blade clattering somewhere in the dark among the niches. The fast one took the wave full in its breastbone and staggered, sternum cracked, one arm hanging by threads of dried sinew—still standing, barely, still fixed on him. He tried to sidestep. He was slow, and bleeding, and it was not. The bony fist caught him across the temple, and the world went sideways. His staff rang on the stone. He went down with it, cheek to the cold flags, dust in his mouth, and the gallery tilted and settled around him: the niches, the ember-eyes close above, the soundless working of a dead jaw. Then even the cold was only a thing he knew, not a thing he felt. The dark of the catacombs closed over him without ceremony, the way it had for everyone else laid here. [ENGINE: Alaric is dead. The second wave tore out of him and the half-ring broke apart. The blade-bearer on his left simply ceased—bones bursting apart mid-swing, the rusted sword ringing off the flags and spinning away. The second came apart a heartbeat later, ribs and skull scattering, its blade clattering somewhere in the dark among the niches. The fast one took the wave full in its breastbone and staggered, sternum cracked, one arm hanging by threads of dried sinew—still standing, barely, still fixed on him.

He tried to sidestep. He was slow, and bleeding, and it was not.

The bony fist caught him across the temple, and the world went sideways. His staff rang on the stone. He went down with it, cheek to the cold flags, dust in his mouth, and the gallery tilted and settled around him: the niches, the ember-eyes close above, the soundless working of a dead jaw. Then even the cold was only a thing he knew, not a thing he felt.

The dark of the catacombs closed over him without ceremony, the way it had for everyone else laid here.

[ENGINE: Alaric is dead. Restless Skeleton C stands over him at 4/54 HP. Combat is over.]
